overview: Apache Parquet is an open-source, columnar storage file format for efficient data processing.
It is optimized for use with big data processing frameworks like Apache Spark and Apache Hadoop.
Parquet stores data in a way that allows for efficient compression and encoding schemes, reducing storage and I/O.
It supports complex nested data structures and provides efficient schema evolution.
learningObjectives: Understand the benefits of columnar storage for analytical workloads.
Identify the key components and internal workings of the Parquet format.
Learn how Parquet optimizes data storage, compression, and query performance.
Recognize suitable use cases and trade-offs for Parquet in data engineering.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Apache Parquet is a self-describing, language-agnostic, columnar storage format designed for efficient data compression and encoding, optimized for analytical queries on large datasets.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine storing a spreadsheet not row by row, but column by column. Parquet does this, allowing you to quickly read only the columns you need for a query, saving time and resources.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Developed jointly by Cloudera and Twitter, Parquet was created to address the need for a more efficient storage format for big data processing, especially for analytical workloads on Hadoop. It became an Apache project in 2013.

whyItMatters.business: Faster analytical queries lead to quicker business insights and better decision-making. Reduced storage and processing costs directly impact the bottom line.
whyItMatters.engineering: Provides a highly efficient, standardized, and interoperable format for data lakes and data warehousing. Optimizes resource utilization for big data pipelines.
whyItMatters.scalability: Its columnar nature and compression techniques allow it to efficiently handle petabytes of data across distributed systems, scaling with data growth.
whyItMatters.cost: Significant cost savings on storage due to high compression ratios and reduced I/O operations. Less compute time translates to lower cloud infrastructure costs.
whyItMatters.reliability: A widely adopted and well-supported open-source standard ensures long-term viability and compatibility across various tools and platforms.

coreComponents.name: File
coreComponents.definition: A complete Parquet file containing data and metadata.
coreComponents.purpose: The top-level container for all Parquet data.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Holds file metadata at the end for efficient reading.

coreComponents.name: Row Group
coreComponents.definition: A logical horizontal partitioning of the data into rows.
coreComponents.purpose: Enables distributed processing, as each row group can be processed independently.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Contains column chunks for a subset of rows.

coreComponents.name: Column Chunk
coreComponents.definition: A chunk of data for a single column within a row group.
coreComponents.purpose: The fundamental unit of columnar storage, allowing individual columns to be read.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Holds all data pages for a specific column in a row group.
coreComponents.examples: All 'sales_amount' values for a row group

coreComponents.name: Page
coreComponents.definition: An immutable, compressed block of data within a column chunk.
coreComponents.purpose: The smallest unit of data read or written, often containing thousands of values.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Applies encoding and compression to a block of column values.

internalWorking: Data is organized into row groups, then each row group's columns are stored separately.
Within each column chunk, data is further divided into pages, which apply encoding (e.g., dictionary, run-length) and compression (e.g., Snappy, Gzip).
File metadata, including schema and statistics for each column chunk, is stored at the end of the file for quick access.
This columnar structure enables 'predicate pushdown' where filtering can occur at the storage level, avoiding reading unnecessary data.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Data is ingested -> Grouped into Row Groups -> Each column in a Row Group is stored as a Column Chunk -> Column Chunks are further divided into Pages -> Pages are Encoded and Compressed -> All components are written to a Parquet file with metadata at the end.
dataFlowWalkthrough: A DataFrame is prepared for writing to Parquet.
The DataFrame is partitioned into 'row groups', typically based on a configurable size (e.g., 128MB).
For each row group, the values of each column are extracted and stored contiguously.
These column chunks are then further broken into 'pages', where various encoding (e.g., dictionary, RLE, bit-packing) and compression algorithms are applied.
Finally, the file's schema and statistics are written as metadata at the end, allowing readers to quickly understand its structure and content.

keyTerminology.meaning: Data is stored column by column, not row by row.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables reading only necessary columns, leading to faster analytical queries and better compression.

keyTerminology.meaning: A horizontal partition of data within a Parquet file.
keyTerminology.importance: Allows parallel processing and efficient skipping of irrelevant data blocks.

keyTerminology.meaning: Filtering data at the storage level before it's loaded into memory.
keyTerminology.importance: Significantly reduces I/O and CPU usage by reading only relevant rows/columns.

importantConcepts.explanation: Parquet supports adding new columns or making existing columns optional without rewriting the entire dataset. This is crucial for evolving data schemas in big data environments.
Parquet employs various compression algorithms (e.g., Snappy, Gzip, Zstd) and encoding schemes (e.g., dictionary, RLE) to drastically reduce file size and improve I/O performance.
Each Parquet file contains rich metadata (schema, statistics) at its footer, enabling efficient query planning and predicate pushdown without reading the entire file.

variationsAndTypes: While Parquet is a single format, its implementation can vary slightly across different processing engines like Apache Spark, Hive, Impala, and Pandas.
Users can choose different compression codecs (Snappy, Gzip, Zstd, LZO) based on desired compression ratio vs. decompression speed trade-offs.
The underlying storage system (HDFS, S3, GCS, local filesystem) does not change the Parquet format itself, but impacts its distributed nature and fault tolerance.
advantages: Efficient Columnar Storage: Reads only necessary columns, reducing I/O and improving query performance for analytical workloads.
High Compression Ratios: Achieves significant storage savings through various encoding and compression techniques.
Predicate Pushdown: Filters data at the storage layer, minimizing data loaded into memory and processed.
Schema Evolution Support: Allows for flexible schema changes (adding columns, making optional) without data migration.
disadvantages: Inefficient for Row-Level Updates: Not suitable for OLTP workloads requiring frequent row-level inserts, updates, or deletes.
Overhead for Small Files: Many small Parquet files can lead to significant metadata overhead and slower query planning.
Complex for Simple Use Cases: For very small, simple datasets, the overhead of Parquet might outweigh benefits compared to CSV.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Best for analytical workloads, data warehousing, and data lakes where large datasets are queried for a subset of columns. Ideal for batch processing and read-heavy scenarios.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid for transactional processing (OLTP), real-time streaming analytics requiring sub-second updates, or when dealing with extremely small, frequently updated datasets.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Imagine a library where instead of storing each book (row) entirely on one shelf, all copies of 'Chapter 1' of every book are on one shelf, all 'Chapter 2' on another, and so on. If you only need to find all titles (one column), you just check the 'Title' shelf, not every book.

commonMisconceptions.reality: Parquet is a file format, not a database. It stores data on disk and is typically accessed by query engines like Spark or Presto.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Parquet is good for all types of data workloads.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Parquet excels in analytical (OLAP) workloads due to its columnar nature, but is inefficient for transactional (OLTP) workloads that require frequent row-level updates.
While Parquet enables compression, individual files should ideally be large (e.g., 128MB-1GB) to optimize performance and reduce metadata overhead in distributed systems.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Parquet's columnar nature and block-level compression allow distributed processing engines to scale efficiently across large clusters for petabyte-scale data.
productionConsiderations.reliability: As an open standard, Parquet is robust and widely supported, ensuring data integrity and compatibility across different big data tools and versions.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: When stored on fault-tolerant file systems like HDFS or object storage like S3, Parquet files inherit the underlying system's fault tolerance capabilities.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Monitor file sizes, number of files, and query performance metrics (scan time, CPU) to ensure optimal Parquet utilization and detect issues like small file problems.
productionConsiderations.security: Leverage underlying storage security (encryption at rest/transit), access control lists (ACLs), and data governance tools to secure Parquet datasets.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Achieves significant cost savings on storage and compute by reducing data footprint and I/O operations through efficient compression and predicate pushdown.
productionConsiderations.performance: Optimized for read performance on analytical queries, particularly when querying a subset of columns. Partitioning and appropriate row group sizes enhance performance.

codeExamples.title: Write a Pandas DataFrame to Parquet
codeExamples.overview: This example demonstrates how to create a simple Pandas DataFrame and save it as a Parquet file.
codeExamples.code:
import pandas as pd

data = {'id': [1, 2, 3], 'name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'], 'value': [100, 200, 150]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

df.to_parquet('output.parquet', index=False)
codeExamples.breakdown: A Pandas DataFrame is initialized. The `to_parquet()` method is then called on the DataFrame to write it to a Parquet file. `index=False` prevents writing the DataFrame index as a column.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A file named 'output.parquet' will be created in the current directory, containing the data in columnar Parquet format.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting `index=False` can add an unnecessary index column. Ensure `pyarrow` or `fastparquet` libraries are installed for Parquet support (`pip install pyarrow`).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For larger datasets, consider specifying compression (`compression='snappy'`) or using PySpark for distributed writes.

codeExamples.title: Read Parquet with Predicate Pushdown using PySpark
codeExamples.overview: This example shows reading a Parquet file with a filter, demonstrating predicate pushdown for efficiency.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("ParquetRead").getOrCreate()

# Assuming 'output.parquet' from previous example exists
df_parquet = spark.read.parquet('output.parquet')

# Apply a filter that Spark can push down
df_filtered = df_parquet.filter(df_parquet['value'] > 120)
df_filtered.show()

spark.stop()
codeExamples.breakdown: A SparkSession is created. The `spark.read.parquet()` method loads the data. The `.filter()` operation allows Spark to leverage Parquet's statistics and predicate pushdown, reading only relevant data.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
A Spark DataFrame showing rows where 'value' is greater than 120:
+---+-------+-----+
| id|   name|value|
+---+-------+-----+
|  2|    Bob|  200|
|  3|Charlie|  150|
+---+-------+-----+
(Actual output may vary based on data and Spark version, but should filter correctly.)
codeExamples.commonIssues: Ensure Spark is configured correctly and the Parquet file path is valid. If the filter column isn't indexed or statistics aren't present, predicate pushdown might be less effective.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For partitioned Parquet files, filtering on partition columns provides the most efficient predicate pushdown. Ensure appropriate row group sizes for optimal scan performance.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retail company needs to efficiently analyze daily sales data to identify top-selling products and regional performance. The raw data arrives as large CSV files.
endToEndExample.architecture: AWS S3 (raw CSV) -> AWS Glue (Spark-based ETL) -> AWS S3 (processed Parquet) -> AWS Athena (query engine).
processingSteps: **Ingestion**: Raw CSV files are uploaded to an S3 'raw' bucket.
**ETL with AWS Glue**: A Glue ETL job reads the CSV files, infers schema, and converts data into a Spark DataFrame.
**Transformation**: The Glue job performs basic cleaning, data type casting, and adds a `dt` (date) column for partitioning.
**Write to Parquet**: The DataFrame is then written back to an S3 'processed' bucket as partitioned Parquet files (e.g., `s3://processed-bucket/sales/dt=YYYY-MM-DD/`).
**Cataloging**: AWS Glue Data Catalog updates with the Parquet table schema and partitions, making it queryable by Athena.
endToEndExample.output: Partitioned Parquet files stored in S3, structured as `s3://processed-bucket/sales/dt=YYYY-MM-DD/part-xxxx.parquet`.
endToEndExample.monitoring: AWS CloudWatch for Glue job metrics (duration, DPU usage). S3 metrics for storage size and access patterns. Athena query logs for performance.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Glue job failure alerts via SNS. Dead-letter queues for failed records during ingestion. Retry mechanisms for S3 writes.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Sales data is available in a highly optimized Parquet format, enabling fast and cost-effective analytical queries using AWS Athena. Business users can quickly generate reports on product performance and regional sales trends.

industryUseCases.problem: Analyzing massive user behavior and streaming data for recommendations and content optimization.
industryUseCases.solution: Storing petabytes of event data, logs, and metrics in Parquet format on S3 and HDFS.
industryUseCases.benefits: Enables efficient querying for machine learning models and data analytics, reducing storage costs and query latency.

industryUseCases.problem: Managing and querying vast amounts of trip data, driver activity, and spatial information for operational insights.
industryUseCases.solution: Utilizing Parquet as a primary storage format in their data lake, often partitioned by time and region.
industryUseCases.benefits: Optimized query performance for critical business intelligence and real-time analytics dashboards, leading to better decision-making.

industryUseCases.problem: Processing user listening habits, music metadata, and ad impression data for personalization and business reporting.
industryUseCases.solution: Standardizing on Parquet for their data lake, leveraging its compression and columnar advantages.
industryUseCases.benefits: Faster data processing with Spark and reduced infrastructure costs for their extensive data analytics platform.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Parquet's columnar nature facilitates horizontal scaling by allowing distributed processing engines to read and process column chunks in parallel across many nodes. Partitioning further enhances this by enabling query engines to prune irrelevant data directories.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: When stored on distributed file systems like HDFS or cloud object storage like S3, Parquet files inherently benefit from the underlying storage's fault tolerance mechanisms, such as data replication and redundancy.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Achieved by storing Parquet files on highly available storage solutions (e.g., S3's multi-AZ redundancy) and using highly available processing engines (e.g., Spark clusters with standby masters).
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Implement cross-region replication for Parquet datasets stored in cloud object storage (e.g., S3 Cross-Region Replication) or backup strategies for HDFS clusters to ensure data recoverability in case of regional outages.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Optimize by choosing appropriate compression codecs (e.g., Snappy for speed, Gzip for ratio), proper partitioning strategies, coalescing small files, and ensuring suitable row group sizes (e.g., 128MB-1GB).
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Leverage high compression to reduce storage footprint. Efficient I/O through columnar reads and predicate pushdown reduces compute time and data transfer costs, especially in cloud environments.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Apply encryption at rest (e.g., S3 SSE, HDFS encryption zones) and in transit. Implement fine-grained access control (e.g., IAM policies for S3, Ranger for HDFS) to secure Parquet files.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Monitor Parquet file sizes, number of files, and data freshness. Track query performance metrics (scan duration, bytes read) from engines like Spark or Athena to identify bottlenecks.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Enforce schema on write (e.g., with Spark's `schema` option) and validate data types. Implement data profiling and checksums to ensure data integrity within Parquet files.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log all write and read operations, including any schema evolution events. Set up alerts for failed writes, unexpected schema changes, or sudden increases in small file counts.

recommendedPractices: Partition data by frequently filtered columns (e.g., `date`, `region`) to enable efficient query pruning.
Choose an appropriate compression codec (e.g., Snappy for balanced performance, Zstd for high compression).
Aim for optimal Parquet file sizes (e.g., 128MB to 1GB) to balance metadata overhead and I/O efficiency.
Coalesce or repartition data before writing to Parquet to avoid the 'small file problem'.
engineeringStandards: Establish consistent schema definitions and enforce data types across all Parquet datasets.
Use descriptive column names that reflect business meaning, avoiding special characters.
Standardize on a single compression codec for a given dataset unless specific performance trade-offs are required.
designRecommendations: Design schemas for analytical queries, placing frequently accessed columns together logically if possible.
Utilize nested types in Parquet for complex data structures instead of flattening them into many columns.
Consider using a columnar data lake format like Parquet for immutable, historical data, and a different system for mutable operational data.
namingConventions: Use lowercase, snake_case for column names.
Include versioning in schema names if complex schema evolution is expected.
documentationStandards: Document the schema of each Parquet dataset, including data types, nullability, and descriptions for each column.
Clearly document partitioning strategies and any compression codecs used for each dataset.
Maintain a data catalog that registers Parquet tables and their locations, such as AWS Glue Data Catalog.
testingStrategies: Validate schema on write and read operations to ensure consistency.
Perform data integrity checks (e.g., row counts, checksums) after writing Parquet files.
Run performance tests with typical queries to ensure the chosen partitioning and file sizes meet latency requirements.

commonMistakes.mistake: Generating too many small Parquet files.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Spark/Flink jobs writing without repartitioning, or streaming jobs writing small batches frequently.
commonMistakes.impact: High metadata overhead for query engines, slow directory listings, and inefficient I/O operations on distributed file systems.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Coalesce or repartition data before writing to achieve optimal file sizes (e.g., 128MB-1GB). Implement compaction jobs for streaming data.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Lack of understanding of query patterns or partitioning by high-cardinality/seldom-filtered columns.
commonMistakes.impact: Query engines cannot use partition pruning, leading to scanning large amounts of irrelevant data and slower queries.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Partition by columns frequently used in WHERE clauses, typically low-cardinality values like `date`, `country`, or `department`.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Defaulting to a codec without considering data characteristics or workload requirements.
commonMistakes.impact: Suboptimal storage size or slower read/write performance depending on the codec choice (e.g., Gzip is slow to decompress, Snappy is fast but less compressed).
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Select codecs based on the trade-off between compression ratio and read/write speed (e.g., Snappy for balanced, Zstd for high compression and good speed, Gzip for maximum compression).

comparisonSection.explanation: Parquet is a columnar, binary format with self-describing schema and rich metadata. CSV is a row-oriented, plain-text format without inherent schema.
Parquet offers superior query performance for analytical workloads due to columnar reads, predicate pushdown, and optimized compression. CSV requires reading entire rows and parsing text.
Parquet achieves significantly higher compression ratios, leading to smaller file sizes and reduced storage costs, through various encoding and compression techniques. CSV offers minimal compression.
Parquet natively supports schema evolution (adding/dropping columns, changing nullability) without data rewrite. CSV has no inherent schema, making schema changes brittle and prone to errors.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is Apache Parquet and why is it used in big data?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Parquet is a columnar storage file format. It's used for big data because it offers efficient storage, high compression, and faster analytical query performance compared to row-oriented formats like CSV.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Focus on columnar storage, compression, and performance benefits for OLAP workloads.

beginnerQuestions.question: Explain the difference between row-oriented and columnar storage.
beginnerQuestions.answer: Row-oriented stores all data for a single row together. Columnar stores all data for a single column together. Columnar is better for analytics as it only reads needed columns.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Use a simple analogy, like a spreadsheet. Mention the I/O benefits for analytical queries.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does Parquet enable 'predicate pushdown'?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Parquet stores metadata and statistics (min/max values) for each column chunk. Query engines use this metadata to skip reading entire row groups or column chunks if they don't satisfy the filter condition.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Detail the role of column statistics and how query planners leverage them to reduce I/O.

intermediateQuestions.question: Describe Parquet's schema evolution capabilities.
intermediateQuestions.answer: Parquet supports non-breaking schema changes like adding new optional columns or making existing optional columns required. It handles this by storing the schema within the file metadata, allowing readers to adapt.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Highlight the flexibility for evolving data schemas without data migration or breaking old readers.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the 'small file problem' in the context of Parquet, and how do you mitigate it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: The small file problem occurs when many tiny Parquet files are generated, leading to excessive metadata overhead for distributed systems. Mitigate it by coalescing or repartitioning data before writing to achieve larger file sizes (e.g., 128MB-1GB).
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Explain the impact on namenodes/metadata stores and query planning. Provide practical solutions like `coalesce()` or compaction jobs.

advancedQuestions.question: You have a large Parquet dataset. How would you optimize it for common analytical queries involving aggregations and filters?
advancedQuestions.answer: I'd partition the data by frequently filtered, low-cardinality columns. Ensure optimal file sizes (128MB-1GB) by repartitioning. Use an efficient compression codec like Snappy or Zstd. Also, consider column ordering if certain columns are always accessed together.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Cover partitioning, file sizing, compression, and even column ordering within the schema for locality.

advancedQuestions.question: Discuss the trade-offs between different compression codecs available for Parquet.
advancedQuestions.answer: Different codecs offer trade-offs between compression ratio and CPU cost for compression/decompression. Snappy is fast but lower ratio. Gzip offers high ratio but is slower. Zstd provides a good balance. The choice depends on storage costs vs. query latency requirements.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Compare Snappy, Gzip, and Zstd, detailing their typical use cases based on performance vs. storage.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A new data pipeline needs to ingest TBs of daily clickstream data and make it available for ad-hoc SQL analysis. How would you recommend storing this data efficiently?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The key is TBs of daily data and ad-hoc SQL analysis. This points to OLAP. Parquet is ideal. Need to consider partitioning for efficient queries and file size management due to high volume.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: I would recommend storing the clickstream data in Parquet format. I'd partition the data by date (e.g., `dt=YYYY-MM-DD`) and potentially by a higher-level identifier like `country` if queries frequently filter by it. I'd ensure the Spark jobs writing the data output Parquet files of optimal size (e.g., 128MB-1GB) by repartitioning before writing, to avoid the small file problem. Snappy compression would be a good choice for balanced performance.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a data lake ingestion layer for various semi-structured data sources (JSON, CSV) into a unified analytical store.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Utilize a batch/streaming ingestion layer (e.g., Spark or Flink) that reads raw JSON/CSV from a landing zone in object storage, validates and conforms the schema, and writes the cleaned output as partitioned, columnar Parquet files into a curated zone. Store rich footer metadata (schema, per-column min/max statistics) so downstream engines like Athena, Presto, or Spark can leverage column pruning and predicate pushdown. Register tables in a metastore (e.g., AWS Glue Data Catalog) for SQL access.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Parquet's columnar format excels at read-heavy analytical queries but is poorly suited to row-level updates, so late-arriving or mutable records require rewrite or a table format like Delta/Iceberg layered on top. Smaller row groups improve fine-grained pruning but add metadata overhead, while larger row groups improve compression and scan throughput at the cost of pruning granularity. Heavier codecs (Gzip, Zstd) shrink storage but raise CPU cost versus Snappy.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Partition data by frequently filtered, low-cardinality columns (e.g., date, region) to enable directory-level partition pruning. Target row-group and file sizes of roughly 128MB-1GB to avoid the small-file problem and run periodic compaction jobs. Let distributed engines read independent row groups and column chunks in parallel across the cluster, scaling compute horizontally as data volume grows.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Apache Parquet is an open-source, columnar, self-describing storage format optimized for compression and analytical (OLAP) queries on large datasets.
keyConcepts: Columnar storage: data stored column-by-column, enabling column pruning (read only needed columns).
Layout: File -> Row Groups -> Column Chunks -> Pages, with schema and statistics in the footer.
Predicate pushdown: per-column min/max stats let engines skip row groups that fail a filter.
Encoding & compression: dictionary, RLE, bit-packing plus codecs like Snappy, Gzip, Zstd.
Schema evolution: add/optional columns without rewriting existing data; default DE columnar format.
formulas: N/A - Parquet is a storage format, not formula-based; key tuning knob is row-group size (target ~128MB-1GB).
interviewPoints: Explain columnar vs row-oriented storage and why columnar wins for OLAP.
Describe the File/Row Group/Column Chunk/Page hierarchy and the footer metadata.
Explain predicate pushdown via column statistics and partition pruning.
Discuss compression codec trade-offs (Snappy vs Gzip vs Zstd).
Address the small-file problem and how to mitigate it.
quickNotes: Parquet is a file format, not a database; queried by engines like Spark, Presto, Athena.
Great for read-heavy analytics; bad for OLTP row-level updates.
Target file/row-group sizes of ~128MB-1GB; avoid many tiny files.
Snappy is the common balanced default; Zstd for higher compression with good speed.

keyTakeaways: Parquet is a columnar, self-describing storage format that reads only the columns a query needs, slashing I/O for analytical workloads.
Its File -> Row Group -> Column Chunk -> Page layout, with footer schema and per-column statistics, enables column pruning and predicate pushdown.
Efficient encoding (dictionary, RLE, bit-packing) and pluggable codecs (Snappy, Gzip, Zstd) deliver high compression ratios and lower storage cost.
Parquet supports schema evolution and is the de facto default columnar format for data lakes, far outperforming row formats like CSV for OLAP.
Tune row-group/file sizes (~128MB-1GB) and partition by common filter columns; it is unsuited to OLTP row-level updates.
